extracted.intended_audience: HSC Standard/Advanced English students preparing Module C reflective writing (Australian HSC)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing a Band 6 reflective text for HSC English Module C: instructs students how to structure an introduction, body and conclusion, what reflective features to include, and how to analyse and justify stylistic choices with examples from their own creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — features of a reflective text
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection: 'The thought process by which students develop an understanding and appreciation of their own learning. This process draws on both cognitive and affective experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features to include: use of first person to express self-assessment; use of evaluative language (e.g. 'my metaphor was effective in...'); considered use of examples (quoting your own work); use of anecdotal references, imagery or metaphor; explanation, description or justification of the use of specific language or stylistic devices; connections between what students learn about writing and the writing that they craft; self-awareness of the learning process. The reflection is designed to get you critically thinking about your own writing choices and to justify stylistic choices to the marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer the question / keep focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your reflection 'answers the question' and maintains a focus on the prompt — e.g. justify how stylistic choices demonstrate a specified concept (hope, anticipation, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the reflection like an essay with a logical structure and a strong 'thesis' and linking sentences that connect back to the question. If the question doesn't require you to reference your text, you may omit explicit references, but you must throughout explore your stylistic choices and link them to how they communicate the required idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction structure — three required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductions should consist of three things, ideally split into three sentences: the aim and purpose of your piece; how you were influenced by your prescribed text; and how through this influence you made stylistic choices to communicate your purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided template: 'My (insert text type) (insert title) aims to (insert key message). I was influenced by (prescribed text and author) whose (what did the author do that influenced you?) to explore (their key message). Hence, by mirroring their use of (stylistic devices) I employed (your main techniques) to (connect back to your purpose).' Example intros are given (e.g. referencing Kafka and naming the techniques you mirrored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing prescribed text (optional but useful)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can reference your prescribed text to show influence on your stylistic choices; however, if the question does not ask for it you will not be penalised for omitting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing the prescribed text can strengthen your reflection by explicitly linking influence -> technique -> purpose. If included, state what the author did that influenced you and which devices you mirrored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralise around macro narrative elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground your reflection by centralising discussion around three macro narrative elements: Characterisation, Setting, Tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: how did you use language (syntax, metaphors, alliteration, dialogue) to create a certain character/setting/tone? How did creating this particular character/setting/tone influence the message you wanted to communicate? The page notes this isn't the only approach but is a useful organising framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body paragraph structure — macro to micro analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure body paragraphs around two or three big (macro) stylistic choices and within each paragraph use quotes that display the micro techniques you used to develop those macros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare at least 2 body paragraphs (3 if you want extra preparation). Example structures: first paragraph on setting, second on tone and characterisation; or first on use of irony then on motif. For each macro device, include micro devices (syntax, metaphor, imagery, dialogue) and quote lines from your text as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use considered examples and quotes from your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Include quoted excerpts of your own creative piece to illustrate the micro techniques that realise your macro choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted examples should be used to show how a technique functions (e.g. 'The imperative metaphor “I am an amalgamation of tales” portrays...'). Explain the effect of each quote and how it contributes to your stated purpose or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify stylistic choices — link technique to effect/message
rubrics_metrics.description: You must explain and justify how each stylistic choice contributes to the communication of your intended idea or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely name devices; analyse their function and link them back to your key message (for example, how irony, imagery or syntax create hope/anticipation). Show the causal path: device -> textual effect -> thematic/message effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective tone and first-person perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a reflective tone and write in the first person to express self-assessment and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasises that reflection should sound like analysis but in first person and with a tone of reflection (very important). Use evaluative language (e.g. 'my metaphor was effective in...') and self-aware commentary about your process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PEEL as paragraph scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) remains a useful structure for paragraphs in reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point = claim about a macro stylistic choice; Evidence = quoted excerpt from your work; Explanation = micro-level analysis of devices and effects; Link = back to the question/purpose. The author explicitly recommends 'PEEL is still your best friend here.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion — concise restatement and linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions should be brief (one or two sentences) and address four key points from the introduction: restate aim/purpose, influence from prescribed text, main stylistic choices, and connect back to the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the template: 'Ultimately, by drawing upon the [stylistic device 1] and [stylistic device 2] used in [prescribed text], I have effectively conveyed [your key message].' The page notes that for a Band 6 you should already have drawn conclusions across body paragraphs, so the conclusion merely summarises and reconnects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph/answer length and exam pragmatics
rubrics_metrics.description: Exam practicality: prepare 2 body paragraphs for typical reflections; 3 only if expecting a heavily weighted question — those are rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guidance links to mark distribution expectations; templates and rehearsal are recommended so you can focus on analysis in the exam rather than structure. Use a template in exams to save time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro vs micro device distinction and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify recurring macro stylistic devices (motif, irony, narrative stance, characterisation, setting, tone) and show how they are developed using micro techniques (syntax, metaphor, alliteration, dialogue, imagery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how micro devices work together to develop the macro device across the text (e.g. motif built via repeated imagery and syntactical patterns). Use specific quoted examples and tie development to the thematic aim.
